subject: chemistry
question_text: Write a short note on Brønsted–Lowry acid-base theory.

verification.note: Chapter 7 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.75-79), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. page_header: Chemical Equilibrium, Acids and Bases · 4 marks

steps.label: Brønsted–Lowry acid
lines: The theory was proposed by Brønsted and
Brønsted–Lowry acid: a substance that can
donate a proton (H⁺). A proton donor.
steps.why: The theory replaces the Arrhenius picture with one action — proton transfer — so the acid is defined by what it gives: one H⁺.
common_mistakes: Writing electron-pair acceptor. That is the Lewis acid; the Brønsted–Lowry acid donates a proton.
Giving no example. HCl is the expected one.
steps.memory_tip: Brønsted acid donates the proton — donor and Brønsted both carry a D sound.
steps.margin_note: Proton donor — two words that carry the mark.

steps.label: Brønsted–Lowry base
lines: Brønsted–Lowry base: a substance that can
accept a proton (H⁺). A proton acceptor.
steps.why: The base is the receiving end of the same proton transfer — every transfer needs one donor and one acceptor, so the two definitions come as a pair.
common_mistakes: Writing that a base must contain OH⁻. NH₃ has no OH⁻ and is still a base — it accepts a proton.
Writing electron-pair donor, which is the Lewis base definition.
steps.memory_tip: The base catches the proton the acid donates — one transfer, two roles.
steps.margin_note: Water appears in both lists — it can donate or accept a proton.

steps.label: The example
lines: NH₃ accepts a proton, so it is the base.
H₂O donates a proton, so it is the acid.
steps.why: This example is chosen because water acts as the ACID in it — proof that the theory assigns roles per reaction, not per substance.
common_mistakes: Labelling H₂O as the base out of habit. In this reaction water donates the proton, so it is the acid.
Writing the equation with a one-way arrow instead of ⇌.
steps.memory_tip: Follow the proton: it leaves H₂O and lands on NH₃. The giver is the acid.
steps.margin_note: Label the acid and the base under the equation.

steps.label: Conjugate pairs
lines: NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of the base NH₃.
OH⁻ is the conjugate base of the acid H₂O.

lines.text: Acid = proton donor; base = proton acceptor

steps.why: After the transfer, each species has a partner one proton away — the conjugate pairs are what the theory adds beyond the bare definitions, so a short note must mention them.
common_mistakes: Pairing NH₃ with OH⁻. The pairs are NH₃/NH₄⁺ and H₂O/OH⁻ — one proton apart each.
Ending the note without the conjugate-pair idea, which is the fourth mark.
steps.memory_tip: Two pairs per equation, each one proton apart. Find them by adding or removing H⁺.
steps.margin_note: Box the donor/acceptor line as the summary of the theory.

insider_note: The single NH₃-in-water equation with all four species labelled — acid, base, conjugate acid, conjugate base — carries half of the marks.
